finding.claim: iconUrl is stored with no validation and later fetched server-side by the nightly sync job. An attacker can set it to an internal or cloud-metadata URL such as http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ or an internal service, and the server will issue a GET to it. Any scheme that java.net.http.HttpClient supports is accepted (http or https), with no host or IP restriction. The response body is read into a byte array, so a later feature that exposes the icon would reflect the response. Even without that, the request is a blind SSRF.
finding.source: The `icon` parameter of Profile.update(webhook, icon), reached via PUT /profile (Profile.java:11).

trace.note: PUT /profile handler update(webhook, icon) receives attacker-supplied icon string
Only `webhook` is checked against the regex; `icon` is never validated
this.iconUrl = icon stores the raw attacker value
Nightly sync() passes URI.create(iconUrl) to HttpClient.send as a GET, so the server makes the request

finding.guards_checked: No scheme, host, or IP allowlist or blocklist on iconUrl. The regex at line 12 covers only webhookUrl. There is no DNS pinning or egress filtering in this code. The default java.net.http.HttpClient does not follow redirects (Redirect.NEVER) unless the caller configures it, but that does not limit a direct request to an internal address. The webhookUrl sink at line 21 was checked and is not exploitable: String.matches() requires a full match of a fixed https://hooks.example.com/ prefix plus exactly 20 alphanumerics, which leaves no room for userinfo, other host, port, or path tricks.

verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:16 stores the unvalidated `icon` (only `webhook` is regex-checked at line 12), and src/Profile.java:23 passes it to URI.create and HttpClient.send as a GET with no scheme or host restriction. The path is only the PUT /profile comment at line 10 and the `sync` method; the repo has no handler or middleware code, so the caller's authentication is not visible.
